title: Machine Learning & AI
summary: Learning functions from data. Two thresholds: optimisation (a model is a loss surface you walk downhill) and generalisation (only performance on unseen data counts). Everything from linear regression to transformers sits on those two ideas.
sources: Bishop: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning
Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman: The Elements of Statistical Learning
Vaswani et al.: Attention Is All You Need (2017)

nodes.label: Data, Features & Splits
nodes.summary: Examples, features and labels, split into training, validation and test sets that never leak into each other.
nodes.outcome: Split a dataset correctly and explain what each split is for.
nodes.check: What is the test set for, and when may you look at it?
nodes.answer: Estimating performance on unseen data; only once, at the very end, after all choices are made.

nodes.label: Linear Regression & Loss
nodes.summary: Fit a line by minimising mean squared error; the loss function defines what 'good' means.
nodes.outcome: Fit a linear model and interpret its loss.
nodes.check: Why is mean squared error sensitive to outliers?
nodes.answer: Errors are squared, so one large error dominates the sum.

nodes.label: Gradient Descent
nodes.summary: Step against the gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate. Troublesome because learning becomes an optimisation trajectory rather than a formula.
nodes.outcome: Run gradient descent by hand for two steps and choose a learning rate.
nodes.check: What happens if the learning rate is far too large?
nodes.answer: The steps overshoot the minimum and the loss oscillates or diverges.

nodes.label: Overfitting & Generalisation
nodes.summary: A model can memorise its training data and fail on new data; the bias–variance trade-off governs model complexity.
nodes.outcome: Diagnose overfitting from training and validation curves.
nodes.check: Training error keeps falling while validation error rises. What is happening?
nodes.answer: Overfitting: the model is fitting noise in the training data and generalising worse.

nodes.label: "Higher training accuracy means a better model"
nodes.summary: Training accuracy rewards memorisation; only held-out performance measures what the model will do in use.
nodes.outcome: Choose between two models using validation, not training, scores.
nodes.check: Model A: 99% train, 70% validation. Model B: 88% train, 86% validation. Which do you deploy?
nodes.answer: Model B: it generalises better; A is overfitting.

nodes.label: Regularisation
nodes.summary: Penalise complexity (L2, L1, dropout, early stopping) to trade a little bias for much less variance.
nodes.outcome: Add L2 regularisation and explain its effect on the weights.
nodes.check: What does an L2 penalty do to a model's weights?
nodes.answer: It shrinks them toward zero, smoothing the model and reducing variance.

nodes.label: Classification & Logistic Regression
nodes.summary: Predict a class probability with a sigmoid or softmax, trained with cross-entropy.
nodes.outcome: Train a logistic classifier and read its decision boundary.
nodes.check: Why use cross-entropy rather than squared error for classification?
nodes.answer: It heavily penalises confident wrong probabilities and gives better gradients for sigmoid/softmax outputs.

nodes.label: Evaluation Metrics
nodes.summary: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC–AUC: choose the metric that matches the cost of each kind of error.
nodes.outcome: Choose a metric for an imbalanced problem and justify it.
nodes.check: 99% of transactions are legitimate. A model predicts 'legitimate' every time. What is its accuracy, and why is that useless?
nodes.answer: 99% accuracy, but recall for fraud is zero: it never catches a single fraud.

nodes.label: "Accuracy is always the right metric"
nodes.summary: On imbalanced data accuracy rewards ignoring the rare class that usually matters most.
nodes.answer: When classes are imbalanced: predicting the majority class scores high while missing every rare case.

nodes.label: Neural Networks
nodes.summary: Layers of weighted sums and nonlinearities; without the nonlinearity, any depth collapses to one linear map.
nodes.outcome: Compute a forward pass through a two-layer network.
nodes.check: Why does a deep network need nonlinear activation functions?
nodes.answer: Without them the layers compose into a single linear function, so depth adds nothing.

nodes.label: Backpropagation
nodes.summary: The chain rule applied backward through the computation graph gives every weight's gradient in one pass.
nodes.outcome: Backpropagate gradients through a small graph by hand.
nodes.check: Which rule of calculus is backpropagation built on?

nodes.label: Convolutional Networks
nodes.summary: Shared local filters exploit spatial structure: translation equivariance with far fewer parameters.
nodes.outcome: Compute a convolution's output size and parameter count.
nodes.check: Why does a CNN need far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer on an image?
nodes.answer: Each filter is small and shared across all positions (weight sharing).

nodes.label: Embeddings
nodes.summary: Discrete items (words, users, products) mapped to vectors where distance reflects similarity.
nodes.outcome: Use cosine similarity on embeddings to find related items.
nodes.check: Why use cosine similarity rather than raw distance to compare embeddings?
nodes.answer: It compares direction and ignores vector length, which often reflects frequency rather than meaning.

nodes.label: Attention & Transformers
nodes.summary: Every token weighs every other token by learned relevance (queries, keys, values). It replaced recurrence and scales with data and compute.
nodes.outcome: Compute scaled dot-product attention for three tokens.
nodes.check: What do the softmax weights in attention decide?
nodes.answer: How much each token's value contributes to another token's output, based on query–key similarity.

nodes.label: Large Language Models
nodes.summary: Transformers pre-trained to predict the next token, then tuned with instructions and human feedback.
nodes.outcome: Explain pre-training, fine-tuning and RLHF and what each changes.
nodes.check: What objective is a base language model pre-trained on?
nodes.answer: Predicting the next token in text.

nodes.label: "The model understands like a person"
nodes.summary: Fluent output comes from statistical next-token prediction; it can be confidently wrong, so outputs need verification.
nodes.outcome: Design a check that exposes a fluent but wrong answer.
nodes.check: Why can an LLM state a false fact confidently?
nodes.answer: It generates plausible continuations from patterns in training data, not from verified knowledge, so fluency is not evidence of truth.

nodes.label: Reinforcement Learning
nodes.summary: An agent learns a policy from rewards by trial and error, balancing exploration and exploitation.
nodes.outcome: Explain the exploration–exploitation trade-off with a bandit example.
nodes.check: Why must an RL agent sometimes take an action it currently believes is worse?
nodes.answer: To explore: its estimates may be wrong, and only trying actions reveals better ones.

nodes.label: Bias, Fairness & Responsible AI
nodes.summary: Models inherit bias from data and objectives; measure group error rates and document data and limits.
nodes.outcome: Audit a classifier's error rates across groups.
nodes.check: A hiring model is trained on past hiring decisions. What risk does that carry?
nodes.answer: It learns and reproduces historical bias in those decisions.
